newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: High house prices, low inflation not contrary - CSO.
newsitem.headline: High house prices, low inflation not contrary - CSO.

text.p: Ireland's Central Statistics Office said on Thursday that there was no contradiction between the country's rapidly rising house prices and low inflation.
In a statement accompanying the publication of Ireland's June consumer price index, the official measure of Irish inflation, the CSO said the CPI does not reflect changes in mortgage interest costs.

"In line with general international practice the Irish CPI does not reflect changes in house prices because the purchase of a house is considered to be an investment rather than consumer expenditure," the CSO said.
Ireland's June CPI came in higher than expected, up 0.3 percent month-on-month against forecasts of a rise of 0.2 percent.
A year-on-year comparison was not available due to lack of comparable data in 1996.
On a 13-month basis, the index rose 1.8 percent from May 1996.

Official housing statistics for the first quarter, 1997, showed second-hand house prices up 18 percent on the same period in 1996 on a national basis and more than 20 percent higher in the Dublin area.

The CSO said house price changes are taken into account in determining the level of new current mortgages but down payments and mortgage capital repayments are not taken into account as they are considered to be an investment.
Changes in mortgage interest costs are estimated by tracking the change in the interest payments for a basket of mortgages of up to 20 years duration, the CSO said.
It said the CPI also covers other home ownership expenses such as repairs and decorations, local authority changes and house insurance.

"Because of the variability in the treatment of home ownership costs and differences in the incidence of owner-occupied and rented dwellings in different countries the International Labour Office recommends that international comparisons of CPIs should be completed exclusive of all housing costs," the CSO said.

The June figures showed the European harmonised index of comsumer prices (HICP), which is designed to measure inflation for EU states on a comparible basis, was up 0.3 percent on the month and 1.7 percent for the 13 months from May 1996.
The CSO pointed out that the HICP excludes home ownership costs at present and efforts were continuing to get an agreement on a harmonised approach.
